kicker: One photo, metres, and a splat

steps.say: One photograph of a court hall. Over half a million Gaussians, made in one pass.

steps.caption: Black: nothing was placed there
steps.say: Swing a little to the side, and the scene holds. Swing further, and black opens behind every pillar.

scenes.headline: Where the metres come from
scenes.sub: Depth Pro 2, its focal estimator, and SHARP's single-photo splats
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Bokeh. A photo tells a network how big things look. How far away they are comes from somewhere else.

steps.say: Apple's Depth Pro 2 predicts metric depth for photos and video, sharp at the edges and steady from frame to frame.
It comes in four sizes, from twenty-four million to eight hundred seventy-two million parameters.
One transformer runs over every frame at the input's own resolution. No tiles, no squashing into a square.

steps.caption: Attention within, then across frames
steps.say: After the first third of its blocks, frames start attending to each other. That is what keeps video steady.
Single-frame methods are sharp and jittery. Video methods are steady and blurry. Depth Pro 2 sits alone at the top right.

scenes.title: What a wrong focal length does

legend: The network sees how big things look

steps.say: The network outputs inverse depth divided by the focal length. That is how big things look, which is all one photo holds.
steps.term: Focal length: pixels per unit of angle

steps.say: Multiply by a focal length to get metres. Thirty percent too long, and the room comes out thirty percent deeper.
Too short, and it squashes toward the camera.
The width never moves. Sideways position doesn't depend on the focal length at all. A wrong one stretches the scene along the view.
Here it is on Depth Pro 2's real depth for the hall, seen from above.

steps.caption: Width readout: unchanged
steps.say: Longer pushes the room away, shorter pulls it in. The width readout doesn't change.
And this is SHARP's thirty millimetre default, for a photo with no EXIF.

scenes.title: Focal estimator, median error
scenes.say: So the focal length matters. Depth Pro 2 ships a twenty-three point five million parameter estimator. On ordinary photos its median error was one point four percent. At the extremes it drifts. A fixed thirty millimetres is far worse.

steps.say: I scored the largest model against Kinect depth on twenty-four frames, with the calibrated focal length.
On average, eight point one percent relative error. But the scale isn't constant.
Near things come out six percent close, far things seven percent far. At six metres, that's forty-two centimetres.
SHARP is the splat model from the viral clip. It is Apple's, from December twenty twenty-five, built on the first Depth Pro.

steps.caption: Two layers of 768 by 768 Gaussians
steps.say: Two depth layers become two Gaussians per two-by-two pixels, and a decoder corrects every one. One million, one hundred seventy-nine thousand, six hundred forty-eight in all.
Every Gaussian sits on a ray of the input camera.

steps.caption: Red: rays that meet no Gaussian
steps.say: Move the camera, and rays slip behind edges. The second layer can fill some of that.
Move further, and nothing was ever placed there.
On my six photos, nine in ten second-layer Gaussians sit within one percent of the first layer's depth.

steps.caption: A reflection in glass, painted on a flat wall
steps.say: And glass is a picture on a wall. The hills reflected here are flat.
That's fine for what SHARP is for: a photo you can lean into, on a headset.
Its depth scales exactly with the focal length it's handed, so the estimator is the piece worth adding.
SplatLab edits splats of multi-view scans: label, lift out, fill the floor.
From one photo there is no floor behind the table to find.

scenes.text: One photo gives you the width. The focal length gives you the depth. Record where it came from.

scenes.say: One photo gives you the width. The focal length gives you the depth. Keep it, and record where it came from.
